_comment: FINAL Telugu tokenizer (Model H). Trained on the FULL training split only, never on validation or test, so held-out fertility and Phase 2 perplexity are not optimistically biased.
_choice: 8,000 pieces, chosen from a 6k/8k/10k/12k sweep measured on held-out validation text. See _why_8000 below.
_why_8000: Phase 2 fixes the model at ~25M parameters and the embedding matrix is
inside that budget, not outside it. At d_model=384 with a tied output
head the embedding costs vocab x 384, and each Transformer block costs
12 x 384^2 = 1,769,472. Vocabulary is therefore bought directly out of
depth.
Measured on held-out validation text:
vocab  chars/tok  fertility  unk rate  vocab used  embedding  layers
The trade is a step function rather than a smooth curve. 6k and 8k both
afford twelve layers; 10k and 12k afford eleven. Within twelve layers 8k
strictly dominates 6k -- 5.7% better compression, higher utilisation,
identical depth -- so 8k is the best tokenizer available at no cost in
layers. Going on to 10k buys 4.0% fertility for a whole Transformer
block.
Unknown-token rate is 0.000% at every candidate, so it cannot
discriminate; byte_fallback covers the tail. Fertility and compression
against parameter cost decide.
Model L (Assamese) selects 8,000 by the same rule on its own measured
sweep. Holding the vocabulary size equal across the two models is a
methodological gain for Phase 3: with granularity constant, a Model H
versus Model L difference is attributable to the DATA rather than to one
model having a coarser tokenizer than the other. The two vocabularies
remain entirely separate and are trained on separate corpora.
_supersedes: This replaces a 32,000-piece tokenizer chosen from a 8k-64k sweep on
held-out fertility alone. That selection was sound on compression and
wrong on budget: 32,000 spends 12,288,000 parameters, 53% of a ~25M
model, leaving only seven Transformer layers. The reported Phase 1
figure of 522,289,581 training tokens was measured with that tokenizer;
the count under 8,000 is higher, because a smaller vocabulary segments
the same text into more pieces. The corpus is unchanged -- only the
_max_sentence_length_note: SentencePiece's limit is in BYTES and defaults to 4,192. Telugu costs three bytes per character, so the exporter's 2,000-character chunks reach ~6,000 bytes and would be dropped SILENTLY. Measured here, the default discarded 0.72% of lines but 7.15% of the text, weighted towards the longest continuous prose - exactly what subword learning depends on.
_input_sentence_size_note: Sentences SentencePiece loads into memory, sampled with shuffle_input_sentence across the whole export. NOT a corpus limit: sample_rate is 1.0, so every document in the training split is exported and eligible to be sampled. Reduced from 3,000,000 after measurement. Telugu sweep candidates peaked at 5.5 GB on a 223.6M-character sample; 3,000,000 sentences loads ~581M characters, which extrapolates to ~14 GB on a 15.8 GB machine. Two candidates had already died with STATUS_DLL_INIT_FAILED (0xC0000142) when memory pressure prevented a process from starting. 1,500,000 loads ~290M characters at roughly 6 GB. For scale, the Assamese final tokenizer learned from 259.7M characters and measured BETTER than its 10%-sample candidate (2.621 vs 2.612 chars/token, fertility 2.001 vs 2.009), so ~290M is ample evidence for the unigram model.
_train_extremely_large_corpus_note: Memory-frugal training path. The training split is 2.29B characters, and the earlier 8k-64k sweep produced std::bad_alloc at 48k on this machine. Slower, but it finishes.
